title: Incident safety basics
summary: Plain-language safety habits for every incident: size-up and situational awareness, protective equipment, accountability and communication, and rest and rehab.
overview: A starter course written by Resgrid in plain language. It is not a substitute for your department's standard operating procedures or for any certification course. Replace the general guidance with your department's own procedures, equipment and terminology before you publish it.

lessons.title: Size-up starts before you arrive
lessons.html:
Safety starts with what you already know: the call type, the address, the time of day, the weather and any notes from the caller. Think about what could hurt you before you arrive.

  • Look for hazards on approach: traffic, power lines, unstable structures, animals, people acting aggressively.
  • Say what you see over the radio so that everyone shares the same picture.
  • If the scene is not safe, stop and wait for the resources you need.

lessons.title: Conditions change
lessons.html:
An incident never stays the same. Keep looking up and around, not only at your task.

  • Notice changes in smoke, sound, structure, traffic and the crowd.
  • Speak up the moment something feels wrong. Anyone may call a stop when they see danger.
  • Know your way out before you need it.

lessons.title: Wear what the task requires
lessons.html:
Your department decides which protective equipment each task requires. Wear all of it, wear it correctly, and keep wearing it until the task is done.

  • Check your equipment at the start of every shift and after every use.
  • Report damaged or contaminated equipment and take it out of service.
  • Add your department's equipment list for each type of incident here.

lessons.title: After the incident
lessons.html:
Contamination does not end when the incident does. Clean yourself and your equipment as your department's procedure describes before you eat, drink or go home.

Report any exposure to your officer so that it can be recorded and followed up.

lessons.title: Who is where
lessons.html:
The person in charge must always know who is on scene, where they are and what they are doing. Use your department's accountability system every time.

  • Check in when you arrive and check out when you leave.
  • Work with a partner and stay together.
  • Answer every roll call.

lessons.title: Radio discipline and emergency traffic
lessons.html:
Keep radio messages short and clear: who you are calling, who you are, and the message. Listen before you talk.

Learn your department's words for emergency traffic and for a member in trouble, and what everyone does when they hear them. Practise them in drills so that they come without thinking.

lessons.title: Rehab is part of the job
lessons.html:
Heat, cold, effort and stress wear people down faster than they notice. Rehab gives members rest, fluids, food and a check of how they are doing before they go back to work.

  • Go to rehab when you are sent, and send others when you see them struggling.
  • Tell the rehab team about any symptoms, however small.

questions.text: Who may call a stop when they see danger?
questions.explanation: Anyone may call a stop the moment they see danger.

questions.text: What should you do with damaged protective equipment?
options: Report it and take it out of service
Keep using it until the incident ends
questions.explanation: Report damaged or contaminated equipment and take it out of service.

questions.text: You should check in when you arrive and check out when you leave.
questions.explanation: The accountability system only works when everyone checks in and out.
